title: Opalytics inference cost sensitivity discovery
summary: Initial discovery with Opalytics exploring per-token economics and hosting options. Customer provided rough traffic and tight budget constraints; discussed batching, prefix/KV caching, quantization, reserved capacity vs hosted burst, and security controls (SOC2, SSO, VPC). Agreed next steps: send detailed pricing worksheet, share SOC2 and network diagram, scope a 1-week perf pilot on Dedicated + hosted fallback.
next_steps: Jordan to send pricing worksheet and sample cost model (by 2026-06-08)
Priya to share Redwood security pack and network diagram (SOC2, SAML, KMS) (by 2026-06-09)
Customer to provide 2 weeks of production trace sample and 95th token size distribution (by 2026-06-12)
Schedule 1-week dedicated perf pilot scope call (week of 2026-06-15)
action_items: Jordan: Send pricing worksheet and example unit-econ spreadsheet - due 2026-06-08
Priya: Share SOC2 report excerpt and VPC peering diagram - due 2026-06-09
Alex: Export 2 weeks of request traces + token histograms - due 2026-06-12
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Blake: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, AE on the Redwood team. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Matt Chen: Matt here — Head of ML at Opalytics.
[00:09] Sara Ortiz: Sara, CTO.
[00:11] Alex Romero: Alex, platform engineering.
[00:14] Priya Nair: Priya from Redwood, I'm the solutions engineer.
[00:18] Jordan Blake: Great. The goal today is to understand your usage and budget constraints around inference so we can recommend hosted, dedicated or private options and give a per-token unit economics picture.
[00:28] Matt Chen: Yeah, thanks. We're trying to move several customer-facing features to real-time LLM scoring, the tricky part is cost. We have a hard cap on ops spend for the next 12 months.
[00:36] Sara Ortiz: To add, some of this is PII-adjacent — not full PHI but sensitive — so we'll need clarity on residency and encryption. We're open to hosted if we can mitigate residency concerns or must go private.
[00:47] Priya Nair: Totally understandable. Quick question on workload shape: what's your expected RPS and typical output length?
[00:52] Matt Chen: Ballpark: peak 120 RPS during business hours, average 45 RPS. Most completions are small — 30 to 120 tokens response, prompts average 80 tokens. So roughly 100 tokens per request end-to-end.
[01:04] Alex Romero: And we expect growth — maybe 2x in six months if a feature launches well.
[01:08] Jordan Blake: Good. On that profile, per-token pricing and batching/ahead caching will drive a lot of the unit cost. For us a few levers matter: per-token list price (hosted), reserved capacity commitments (dedicated), batching window configuration, and prefix/KV caching for repeated context.
[01:22] Sara Ortiz: Can you walk through an apples-to-apples comparison? Like if we do hosted at list vs dedicated with a 6–12 month commit.
[01:29] Priya Nair: Sure. Very high-level: hosted per-token is simplest — you pay for tokens consumed and get our multi-tenant SLA. For sustained throughput, dedicated can be 30–50% lower per-token after amortizing reserved GPU capacity, because you avoid multi-tenant overhead and can use higher batch sizes. Private (VPC/on-prem) is similar to dedicated price-wise but adds infra/Ops costs and a platform fee.
[01:46] Matt Chen: Do you have example math?
[01:48] Jordan Blake: Example: take 100M tokens/month. Hosted baseline might be $0.0009 per input token and $0.0018 per output token (example figures, we'll send exact worksheet). That gives ~ $2700 for inputs + $1800 for outputs = $4500. With batching and prefix caching that's reducible — if you get 20% token reuse via KV/prefix and 20% savings from batching and quantization, you could be down to ~$2700.
[02:15] Alex Romero: Wait, the hosted list price you quoted — is that for a particular model size?
[02:18] Priya Nair: Right, sorry — numbers map to a medium decoder model. For larger context or bigger models the per-token rate increases; but dedicated lets you pin model variants and use optimized kernels/quantization to cut runtime cost.
[02:29] Sara Ortiz: You mentioned KV cache — how often would that realistically apply for us? Our prompts change per customer but we have a large shared system prompt and a lot of repeated metadata.
[02:38] Priya Nair: That's a perfect fit. If you keep a stable system prompt or repeated few-shot examples, Redwood's prefix caching stores the KV-cache for those prefixes so you don't pay compute for the cached tokens. Operationally, you get big savings on long contexts. If 40% of the tokens are stable prefix across calls, that can be a huge delta.
[02:55] Matt Chen: Ok, good. On latency: our p50 target is 120ms, p95 under 300ms. Is that realistic with dedicated?
[03:03] Jordan Blake: Yes. Hosted commonly achieves p50 around 60–150ms depending on model and sequence length, p95 depends on burst and availability. Dedicated gives more predictable p95 because you control GPU pools and batch windows and can allocate smaller max-batch sizes to meet tail latency. We also support autoscale + burst capacity policies.
[03:20] Alex Romero: For private deployments we need VPC peering + KMS integration — do you support customer-managed keys?
[03:26] Priya Nair: Yes, for Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integration for key isolation, and we can do VPC peering or private link. We'll share the network diagram.
[03:35] Sara Ortiz: SOC 2?
[03:36] Jordan Blake: SOC 2 Type II available; Priya will send the security pack after the call.
[03:39] Priya Nair: I'll attach the SOC2, the pen test summary, and our typical VPC peering diagram. Also SAML SSO via Okta is supported for admin console.
[03:47] Matt Chen: Great. Another constraint: our budget owner wants a hard monthly cap. If traffic spikes we need automatic fallback to cheaper models or reject requests not to blow budget. Is there a routing policy for that?
[03:58] Priya Nair: Yup. Redwood supports routing by cost/tier. You can configure a policy: primary route to high-quality model on Dedicated, fallback to a smaller / quantized variant on Hosted or to cached response. We can also set hard rate limits or budget gate that returns a throttled response.
[04:14] Jordan Blake: Typically teams do a blended approach: Dedicated for steady-state traffic, hosted for bursting, with a fallback model chain to manage cost. That way you get the latency predictability for steady traffic and avoid over-provisioning for spikes.
[04:25] Alex Romero: How quick is burst to hosted — like is there cross-region latency concerns?
[04:29] Priya Nair: We try to colocate dedicated pools near your region; bursting is immediate to a compatible hosted model in the same region where available. If you need hard residency we can route to a private fallback or configure queueing instead of cross-region bursting.
[04:44] Matt Chen: For our finance team, we need a model that shows per-customer unit economics so they can forecast per-feature spend. Can you provide a sample sheet where we plug in tokens per call, calls/day, reuse rates, and get monthly cost?
[04:55] Jordan Blake: Yes — that's the pricing worksheet we'll send. It includes fields for tokencounts, batch size, cache hit rate, quantization factor, and maps to hosted vs dedicated cost buckets.
[05:03] Sara Ortiz: We're risk-averse about sending anything that could be PII to hosted. If we do a pilot, what minimal data set would you need?
[05:10] Priya Nair: For initial perf estimates, anonymized traces with query lengths and token histograms are usually enough. For quality/regression tests, sampled prompts with redactions are fine. Also, we can run the pilot entirely in Private VPC if that's required, but that adds setup time.
[05:24] Matt Chen: Let's talk numbers. Our finance limit is roughly $25k/month for this initiative to start. Given our expected 100 tokens/request and 45 RPS average — does that fit hosted or dedicated?
[05:35] Jordan Blake: Quick back-of-envelope: 45 RPS average ~ 3.9M requests/day ~ 118M requests/month (wait math check) — sorry let me recalc, 45 RPS * 3600 * 24 = 3,888,000 requests/day; monthly ~ 116M requests. At 100 tokens/request that's 11.6B tokens/month — OK that's huge, so maybe you meant 45 RPS aggregated across a smaller subset?
[05:59] Matt Chen: Sorry, we meant 45 RPS for the feature subset, which is about 3.9M requests/day — yes that maps to ~120M tokens/day? Hmm, we need to check my numbers, I have token mix per week, will send.
[06:11] Alex Romero: Yeah apologies — we have multiple features, I'm trying to isolate this one. For the pilot let's assume 2M requests/month at 100 tokens => 200M tokens/month.
[06:20] Priya Nair: That's manageable. At 200M tokens/month, hosted could be in the low thousands to high thousands depending on model and cache. Dedicated with a small reserved pool (e.g., 1-2 GPUs depending on model throughput) could bring costs down materially if sustained. The pricing worksheet will show crossover point.
[06:36] Jordan Blake: Also note the impact of batching window: increasing batch window from 10ms to 40ms may drop per-token compute by X% (we'll show numbers); but that will add latency. Trades off cost vs p95.
[06:46] Matt Chen: We're sensitive about p95 though. 200–300ms extra is unacceptable for interactive UI.
[06:50] Priya Nair: Then smaller max-batch sizes and prefix caching become the levers — we can show a configuration that keeps p95 within your targets and still leverages caching to save cost.
[06:59] Sara Ortiz: Any options around quantization/INT8? How does that affect quality?
[07:03] Priya Nair: We support quantized variants for many open models; int8/in4 gives compute/cost improvements but some workloads see small quality regressions. Redwood Optimize suggests per-workload evals — we can run a short quality test on your evaluation prompts to estimate delta.
[07:18] Alex Romero: If we do Dedicated, what's the lead time to stand up a pool?
[07:22] Jordan Blake: Typical onboarding for Dedicated is 2–4 weeks depending on contract and region. Private deployments can be longer, 4–8 weeks including networking and KMS integration. For the pilot we can provision a small dedicated pool or do hosted with config locks.
[07:36] Matt Chen: For the contract team — what's the billing model for dedicated? Monthly reserved + overage?
[07:41] Jordan Blake: Yes reserved monthly commit for base capacity, with configurable burst buckets billed at hosted rates or a reduced overage rate if you select a higher commit tier. We can offer different amortization for multi-month commitments.
[07:52] Sara Ortiz: We may want a 6-month initial commit with quarterly reviews.
[07:56] Jordan Blake: That's common. We'll model that in the worksheet.
[07:59] Priya Nair: Quick note on observability: Redwood Console gives token-level cost breakdown by route and model, you can tag routes by customer to see per-customer spend. That helps drive per-customer chargeback.
[08:12] Alex Romero: Nice. On the security side, can we restrict data retention and purge logs?
[08:17] Priya Nair: Yes, retention policies configurable per workspace/route; Private deployments give the strongest controls with customer retention settings enforced. Hosted can be configured with short retention and export hooks.
[08:29] Jordan Blake: Any other blockers?
[08:31] Matt Chen: Two concerns: 1) Our CFO wants a clear worst-case scenario so they can set the cap. 2) Our ML lead wants to test quality regression on quantized models before any commitment.
[08:40] Priya Nair: Both are straightforward. We will provide a worst-case cost sheet assuming 0% caching, minimal batching, and peak RPS. For quality we can run a short eval harness and a 1-week pilot on a dedicated pool with your eval prompts.
[08:52] Sara Ortiz: About compliance, if we do private deployment on our cloud, do you still need access to logs for support?
[08:58] Jordan Blake: Only with explicit agreement — typically we ask for anonymized telemetry for support but can operate without access; support playbooks differ for private installs. We'll document options in the security pack.
[09:09] Alex Romero: If the pilot shows >20% improvement vs hosted in cost per token, would there be pricing flexibility on committed tiers?
[09:16] Jordan Blake: We can discuss tiered discounts for committed volumes; we'll include sample tiering options in the worksheet.
[09:22] Matt Chen: Ok next steps then?
[09:24] Jordan Blake: To recap — Jordan sends the pricing worksheet and sample unit-econ model by 6/8; Priya sends SOC2, network diagram, and SSO/KMS details by 6/9; Alex to provide two weeks of request traces and token histograms by 6/12; we'll schedule a 30–60 minute pilot scoping call for the week of 6/15.
[09:40] Sara Ortiz: That works. One last quick question: do you have any customers in the same vertical we can reference for similar scale?
[09:47] Priya Nair: Yes, we have references in retail and fintech — I'll send anonymized case notes. Also can provide performance artifacts that show batch/cache savings.
[09:58] Matt Chen: Great. Thanks everyone.
[10:00] Jordan Blake: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the materials.
[10:05] (call ends)

Notes on transcript: occasional mis-transcriptions present ("KVcach" vs KV cache, "ink8" vs int8), some speaker labels approximate. There's natural back-and-forth, qualification on tokens, reuse, budget and SLA tradeoffs.
